paragraphs: Judah ben Gerim. Hyman writes that he was a disciple of Rashbi (רש״בי; supplied דרש״בי), as in Mo'ed Katan (מו״ק) 9b: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai (or Akmai) and Judah ben Gerim studied the section on vows (Parashat Nedarim) at the house of Rashbi. They took leave of him in the evening; in the morning they came back and were taking leave of him again. He said to them: Did you not already take leave of me in the evening? They said to him: You taught us, our master. Rashbi said to his son: These people are men of distinction (lit. men of form); go

to them, that they may bless you. And they blessed him: May it be [His] will that you sow and not reap, that you bring in and not take out, take out and not bring in, that your house be destroyed and your lodging be settled, that your table be thrown into confusion, and that you not see a new year. He did not understand their words, and when he came to his father he said to him: Not only did they not bless me, but they even cursed me. But his father explained to his son that all their words were

precious blessings. The saying is brought in Bereshit Rabbah (ב״ר), supplied פ״לה-ג [ch. 35, §3], and there [the names are] Rabbi Yitzchak, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yudan Giyori; Hyman says that it was corrupted from Judah ben Gerim to Yudan Giyori, or perhaps [he is so called] because he was a son of converts; and in place of Rabbi Yochanan Hyman says the reading should be R′ Yonatan ben Asmai [ב״ע; compare the opening Asmai/Akmai variant]. And in Shabbat 33b (supplied שבת לג:) Hyman relates that once Rashbi (רש״בי) spoke against the Roman government, and Judah ben Gerim (and Rashi explains: he was the son of a male convert and a female convert) was sitting there, and he went and recounted

the words of Rashbi (to his disciples or to his fathers/parents, Rashi), and his words were heard by the government, and because of this Rashbi had to flee, and he and his son stayed thirteen years in a cave. When he came out he found Judah ben Gerim and said: Is this one still in the world? He set his eyes upon him and he became a heap of bones. Hyman reports that Tosafot there does not read “a heap of bones,” but rather “he died” (נח נפשיה).

notes.text: Abbreviation דרש״בי / רש״בי is rendered R. Shimon b. Yochai as a standard reading, not in the frozen registry; kept uncertain. ב״ע (after R. Yonatan) is left in Hebrew, unexpanded: probably Asmai/Akmai, uncertain.

Printed citations (כמו״ק ט:, בב״ר פ״לה-ג, שבת לג:, רש״י, תוס׳) are retained as printed; the colon is read as amud b. No witness supplied; unverified. 'פ״לה-ג' unit numbers not converted to modern numbering without witness.

The final sentence 'אך נח נפשיה' is ambiguous in its relation to Tosafot's reading; the translation is literal and tentative. Also, 'לתלמידיו או לאבותיו' reading of 'אבותיו' (possibly his fathers/parents) is literal.

The consulted William Davidson Moed Katan 9a names Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehudah ben Gerim studying at the house of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, includes “You taught us, our master,” and sends the son for a blessing. The blessings continue on 9b; Hyman’s supplied 9b locator, Asmai/Akmai alternative, quoted negations and parent’s explanation are retained. The digital son says that they distressed him, whereas Hyman says they cursed him. Midrash Rabbah — TE Bereshit Rabbah 35:3 fully names Rabbi Yitzchak, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yudan Giyorei; this supports those local titles without adopting Hyman’s asserted corruption, his alternative explanation from converts, or his proposed Yochanan-to-Yonatan emendation. His “should read” and ב״ע remain visible, and the proposed personal title remains R′. The William Davidson Shabbat 33b narrative has Yehudah ben Gerim report the conversation; its cave account gives twelve years followed by twelve months. The whole selected Shabbat 34a paragraph has the question “Is this one still in the world?” and the heap of bones: this is a positive comparison beside Hyman’s supplied 33b, not a locator correction. The consulted Vilna Rashi on Shabbat 33b explains בן גרים as the son of a male and female convert, and gives “to students or to his father and mother”; Hyman’s “to his disciples or to his fathers/parents” remains his wording. The whole saved Vilna Tosafot comment explicitly rejects the derogatory heap-of-bones reading in favor of נח נפשיה, supporting Hyman’s reported contrast. That comment gives Rabbi Yehudah and names Shimon ben Chalafta as a Moed Katan companion, unlike Hyman’s opening; no parties are identified across the accounts. Its earlier empty default response remains retrieval unavailability, not absence or a newly corrected printed text. All four current notes and three carried original notes remain verbatim, including their earlier uncertainties. These are named digital comparisons, not fresh printed-page or correction-history verification, and the source hold remains.

In the consulted Moed Katan, the double leave-taking and Rabbi Shimon's request to his son begin on 9a, and the blessings continue on 9b. The son there says the men distressed him. Hyman's printed notice says that the son thought they cursed him and that his father explained their words as blessings. Bereshit Rabbah 35:3 gives Rabbi Yitzchak, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yudan Giyori, and offers vows or libations as the topic of study. The proposed changes of names and the alternative explanation from converts are Hyman's.

Hyman's notice (vol. II, p. 559) gives thirteen years in the cave. The consulted Shabbat 33b gives twelve years and then twelve months after the first emergence. In the consulted 34a account the heap of bones follows the encounter with Judah. The consulted Rashi on 33b gives students or his father and mother as the people Judah told, and explains that the government heard the matter through him. The consulted Tosafot prefers “he died” and names Shimon ben Chalafta as Judah's companion in Moed Katan, where the consulted text names Yonatan ben Asmai.
